newsitem.title: USA: AT&T to up some residential, business rates.
newsitem.headline: AT&T to up some residential, business rates.

text.p: AT&T Corp. will increase some residential and business long-distance rates, adding an average 60 cents a month to the typical residential customer's bill, the telecommunications giant announced Wednesday.

AT&T also launched a cut-rate, international call-back service in Tokyo. In a call-back service, users first call a switching centre in the United States and calls are then connected at lower U.S. rates.
AT&T said basic U.S. rates for direct-dialed, state-to-state calls made from a home will rise 5.9 percent, effective Dec. 1.
The New York-based company said it also would raise the average rate of calls made with a calling card by 5 percent and those made with the assistance of an AT&T operator by 2.6 percent.
AT&T said it would raise rates charged small business customers for international, direct-dialed, toll-free by 4.8 percent.

It also said it would increase monthly fees on its Reach Out America, SelectSaver and AnyHour Saver calling plans. AT&T said it stopped selling those plans in 1993 when it introduced its "True" family of calling plans.
The company said it was raising rates to pay for significant investments made to broaden its service line, build technical infrastructure and improve customer service.
The Tokyo call-back service launched Wednesday marked the first time AT&T has started such a service, AT&T Asia/Pacific President John Legere said.
"We are the first major telecommunications carrier in Japan to introduce a low-cost, flat-rate international calling option," Legere said.
AT&T's Japanese unit said it would charge 240 yen ($2) for a three-minute call to Canada or the United States from Tokyo, compared with the 450 yen ($3) Japanese customers now pay.
The service, which at first will be offered only to business customers in Tokyo, could be used for sending data and faxes, Legere said.
